introduction: A process can be alive while users cannot read their tasks. A service-level indicator (SLI) describes one user-visible result; a service-level objective (SLO) sets the acceptable proportion of good results over an explicit window. This lesson turns the measurements from weeks 33–34 into a release decision and an actionable local alert.

Use a learning target of 99.5% successful eligible GET /tasks requests over 30 days. Eligible means the caller supplied a valid lab token and the request reached the service; expected authentication failures and health probes are excluded. Our status-based proxy counts 2xx and 5xx responses and cannot detect requests lost before application instrumentation. Pair it with the external synthetic check from week 33 and record that blind spot.

The short experiment below validates rule behavior, not a month of reliability. Prometheus keeps only 24 hours in this lab, so a real 30-day objective requires a durable measurement system and retention long enough for that window. An alert appearing in the local Alerts page also does not prove that an on-call notification reached a human.
prerequisites: Ubuntu 24.04 Bash in WSL2 or a disposable Linux VM; Docker is running. Use the same terminal unless a step names a second terminal.
Complete weeks 33–34. Keep the local Compose stack and observability/local.env; no Kubernetes or cloud resources are needed.
Know the difference between a counter and a histogram, and keep the synthetic-check script from week 33.

concepts.title: Budget is an allowance of bad events
paragraphs: For a request-based availability SLO, availability is good eligible requests divided by all eligible requests. At 99.5%, the allowed bad fraction is 0.005. One million eligible requests allow 5,000 bad ones; this is not automatically a time-based downtime allowance.

Burn rate is observed bad fraction divided by the allowed bad fraction. A 2% error fraction burns a 0.5% budget at four times its sustainable rate. At constant traffic mix, that would consume a 30-day budget in 7.5 days. Traffic changes make this an estimate, so retain event counts.
concepts.example: 10,000 eligible requests and 75 server failures gives 99.25% availability and 1.5 times burn.
concepts.judgment: Choose targets with users and service owners. Copying another company’s number can create expensive engineering work without improving the user’s important journey.

concepts.title: Alert for an action, not a graph
paragraphs: A page needs an owner, a symptom, an immediate investigation and a bounded mitigation. CPU above a number is only useful when someone can decide what to do. This lab alert says valid task reads are failing and points at request logs, database readiness and recent changes.

Long and short windows answer different questions: sustained consumption and whether the problem is still happening. Low traffic can make one failure dominate a ratio. We require a small minimum event count for this demonstration and separately inspect synthetic checks; that count suppresses some real sparse-traffic incidents.
concepts.example: An elevated 30-minute ratio plus an elevated 5-minute ratio avoids paging long after a brief burst ended.
concepts.judgment: Do not use a quiet application counter as proof of success. Total application failure can stop metric production entirely; scrape availability and an external probe cover different failure modes.

steps.title: Write the objective before the rule
steps.purpose: Make the denominator, target, window and blind spots reviewable.

commands.code:
cd ~/dev-opps-lab/app/taskboard
mkdir -p observability evidence/w35
cat > observability/slo.md <<'EOF'
Journey: an authenticated user lists their tasks.
Eligible proxy: GET /tasks responses with status 2xx or 5xx.
Good proxy: eligible responses with status 2xx.
Availability target: 99.5% over a rolling 30-day window.
Latency target: 95% of successful eligible reads below 500 ms.
Owner: the learner operating this disposable lab.
Exclusions: expected invalid-token requests, health checks and metrics scrapes.
Gaps: requests lost before middleware; no 30-day retention in this lab.
Release rule: investigate sustained budget burn; pause unrelated releases during an incident.
Local alert action: verify impact, inspect readiness/logs/recent changes, then restore the known-good configuration.
EOF
python3 - <<'PY'
total, bad, target = 10000, 75, 0.995
allowance = total * (1-target)
print(f"availability={1-bad/total:.4%}; allowed_bad={allowance:.0f}; burn={(bad/total)/(1-target):.2f}")
PY
explain: mkdir -p creates only these lab folders. The quoted heredoc writes a literal SLO specification; edit the owner to your own name before publishing.
Python computes the observed success fraction, allowable failures and burn from the same request population. This avoids mixing a request SLO with minutes of downtime.
commands.expected: The calculation reports 99.2500%, 50 allowed failures and burn 1.50. The document states what was not measured.
commands.troubleshoot: If your preferred SLI includes client timeouts, add an independent client measurement; application middleware cannot count a request it never received.

steps.checkpoint: Explain why /livez success does not belong in the denominator for a user task-list journey.

steps.title: Install one local alert with a runbook
steps.purpose: Keep expressions and operational response together.

commands.code:
cat > observability/alerts.yml <<'EOF'
groups:
- name: taskboard-lab
  interval: 5s
  rules:
  - alert: TaskReadsFailingLab
    expr: |
      (sum(rate(taskboard_http_requests_total{method="GET",route="/tasks",status=~"5.."}[1m]))
       / sum(rate(taskboard_http_requests_total{method="GET",route="/tasks",status=~"2..|5.."}[1m])) > 0.05)
      and
      (sum(increase(taskboard_http_requests_total{method="GET",route="/tasks",status=~"2..|5.."}[1m])) >= 10)
    for: 20s
    labels:
      severity: lab
    annotations:
      summary: Authenticated task reads are failing in the local lab
      runbook: observability/task-read-runbook.md
EOF
cat > observability/task-read-runbook.md <<'EOF'
1. Record UTC time, affected journey and observed errors.
2. Run the external synthetic check and compare /livez with /readyz.
3. Inspect the app and database service state and recent logs.
4. Check the most recent configuration/image change before changing anything.
5. Restore the known-good dependency/configuration. Do not reset the database volume.
6. Verify authenticated reads, the existing task and synthetic checks.
7. Record recovery time, lingering alert window and follow-up owner.
EOF
python3 - <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path
p=Path("observability/prometheus.yml")
s=p.read_text()
if "rule_files:" not in s: s += "\nrule_files:\n  - /etc/prometheus/alerts.yml\n"
p.write_text(s)
PY
cat > slo.yaml <<'EOF'
services:
  prometheus:
    volumes:
      - ./observability/alerts.yml:/etc/prometheus/alerts.yml:ro
EOF
set -a; . observability/local.env; set +a
docker compose -f compose.yaml -f observability.yaml -f tracing.yaml -f slo.yaml run --rm --no-deps --entrypoint promtool prometheus check rules /etc/prometheus/alerts.yml
docker compose -f compose.yaml -f observability.yaml -f tracing.yaml -f slo.yaml up -d prometheus
explain: cat writes the alert, runbook and an extra Compose mount. The rule requires both more than 5% server failures and at least 10 eligible events in a minute; for: 20s requires the condition to persist. These intentionally short lab windows are not the 30-day objective.
Python appends the rule-file location once to the existing scrape configuration. set -a exports values from the local secret environment file; set +a stops automatic exporting.

Compose merges the same four files in order. run --rm creates a temporary validation container; --no-deps avoids starting dependencies; --entrypoint selects promtool. up -d recreates Prometheus if the mount changed.
commands.expected: promtool reports SUCCESS. http://127.0.0.1:9090/rules shows TaskReadsFailingLab with no evaluation error.
commands.troubleshoot: If the mount file is a directory or the rule is missing, inspect docker compose ... config and the exact observability/prometheus.yml path from week 33. Do not replace the entire scrape config with the alert file.

steps.checkpoint: Identify both the ratio threshold and the minimum volume guard. No Alertmanager or external notification delivery is configured.

steps.title: Generate bounded authenticated traffic
steps.purpose: Create enough real eligible requests to observe the rule.

explain: The environment file supplies the existing token without embedding it in the script. urllib sends one authenticated read per second, at most 120 attempts, each with a three-second timeout.
HTTPError preserves server response codes; connection failures are recorded separately because the server counter cannot see them. tee shows and saves the output without recording the token.
commands.expected: Healthy responses are 200. While this command runs, perform the fault below in a second terminal.
commands.troubleshoot: If every request is 401, check that this terminal loaded the same .env used to create the app. Invalid authentication is excluded from this SLI and is not the intended fault.

steps.checkpoint: Keep healthy, failing and recovered responses in one timestamped record; inspect /alerts in Prometheus during the failure.

steps.title: Distinguish measurement from a monthly claim
steps.purpose: Use a longer-window expression as a design exercise and calculate an example budget.

commands.code:
curl -fsSG http://127.0.0.1:9090/api/v1/query --data-urlencode 'query=sum(increase(taskboard_http_requests_total{method="GET",route="/tasks",status=~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(increase(taskboard_http_requests_total{method="GET",route="/tasks",status=~"2..|5.."}[5m])) / 0.005' | python3 -m json.tool
python3 - <<'PY'
for fraction in (0.005,0.02,0.10):
    burn=fraction/0.005
    print(f"bad={fraction:.1%}, burn={burn:g}, constant-rate days-to-exhaust={30/burn:g}")
PY
explain: curl -G encodes a read-only query in the URL; --data-urlencode protects PromQL punctuation. The expression divides observed error fraction by the 0.005 allowance. python -m json.tool formats the response.
The separate calculation compares sustainable, moderate and fast budget consumption under an explicitly constant-rate assumption.
commands.expected: The example burns are 1, 4 and 20; estimated exhaustion is 30, 7.5 and 1.5 days. A missing query result means missing data, not zero failure.
commands.troubleshoot: If the query returns an empty vector before the first 5xx, generate the bounded fault; Prometheus does not invent an unobserved status series. Keep that missing-series behavior in the design review.

steps.checkpoint: For a production proposal, write a 30m/5m combined rule, its traffic assumptions and notification test; label it unvalidated until enough data and delivery evidence exist.

failure.title: The process is alive but task reads fail
failure.boundary: Only stop the disposable Compose database, for about 45 seconds, while the bounded traffic script runs. Do not delete its volume.

explain: stop sends a graceful termination to this named Compose database service; its volume remains.
inject.expected: /livez remains 200 while authenticated reads and /readyz become 503.
inject.troubleshoot: If no app is running, restore the full week-34 stack first; this drill assumes a healthy baseline.

investigate.code:
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w "live=%{http_code}\n" http://127.0.0.1:8000/livez
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w "ready=%{http_code}\n" http://127.0.0.1:8000/readyz
docker compose ps -a
docker compose logs --tail=20 app
curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:9090/api/v1/alerts | python3 -m json.tool
explain: curl discards bodies and prints status; ps -a includes the stopped dependency; logs limits output to the last 20 lines.
The API lists local alert state. Wait through several scrape/evaluation intervals and the 20-second pending duration, while traffic continues.
investigate.expected: Live 200, ready 503, stopped db and a pending then firing local alert give distinct evidence.
investigate.troubleshoot: If the rule remains inactive, inspect request volume, eligible labels and rules evaluation errors before weakening thresholds.

hints: Compare a process health signal with a user request.
A firing rule can take time to clear because its one-minute window still contains failures.

explanation: Database unavailability breaks the authenticated task-read journey while the Python process continues answering health requests. The runbook should preserve data and restore the dependency before considering a code change.

explain: start restarts the existing database service and its preserved data.
recover.expected: Readiness and task reads recover after PostgreSQL becomes ready.
recover.troubleshoot: Inspect docker compose logs --tail=30 db if readiness remains false; do not erase the volume to make the signal green.

explain: Check the dependency-aware endpoint and a real authenticated journey after loading .env in this terminal.
verification.expected: Both requests return 200; existing tasks remain. The alert resolves after its data window recovers.
verification.troubleshoot: If a task is missing, stop and inspect which database and volume the app uses; availability and data durability are separate checks.

questions.prompt: Why exclude /livez from the task-read SLI?
questions.answer: The health handler does not need PostgreSQL. Including its successes would dilute failures of the journey users care about.

questions.prompt: Does 99.5% request availability mean exactly 216 minutes downtime per month?
questions.answer: No. The request SLO counts requests; traffic can vary by time. A separate time-based SLO could imply that downtime allowance under a defined 30-day window.

questions.prompt: What does a missing counter series mean?
questions.hint: Distinguish no sample from a numeric zero.
questions.answer: It may mean no such label was observed, failed scraping, a stopped process or inadequate history. Check up, target health and the external probe before interpreting it.

questions.prompt: Why might a local alert fail to notify anyone?
questions.hint: Which delivery component did we install?
questions.answer: We installed only a Prometheus rule. Routing, receivers, contact ownership and an end-to-end notification test are separate work.

exercise.brief: Design a slow-burn notification and a fast-burn page for the same task-read journey.
constraints: Keep the same denominator and target.
Do not claim 30-day compliance from this session.
deliverables: Two expressions with long and short windows, a low-traffic policy, a named owner and a runbook.
acceptance: Explain one missed incident and one noisy case for each proposal.
Calculate budget consumption for 1%, 5% and 100% failures.
hints: Start with error fraction divided by 0.005.
Use an AND between sustained and recent windows.
solution: A defensible proposal pages on high burn in both a longer and shorter window, routes lower sustained burn to a ticket, and uses external checks for low/no traffic. Exact windows follow operational response time and business impact. Record how you will test notification delivery.

cleanup.code:
docker compose start db
docker compose ps
explain: Ensure the deliberately stopped dependency is restored; list the service state before finishing.
cleanup.expected: The local stack is healthy and intentionally retained for week 36.
cleanup.troubleshoot: Do not run down -v; the next incident exercise needs the existing task data.

repoConnections.principle: Start reliability work from the user journey and an operational response.
repoConnections.application: The lesson ties an explicit event denominator to a budget, a local alert and a recovery runbook; it requires explaining missing data rather than reading a green dashboard as proof.
A task-read SLI and an external request can disagree when traffic never reaches the service. The drill records both and preserves that gap in the objective.

Local alert display is demonstrated; no external message is sent or configured.
